_metadata.title: Kannada Mitra — Bengali & Urdu Pending Translations Review Dataset
_metadata.description: Structured candidate review data for 54 foundation vocabulary items. Strictly isolated from the active runtime learning dataset. All items require verified review by a native speaker before ingestion into production vocabulary.
_metadata.isolationNotice: This file is exclusively a review manifest. It is NOT loaded into active vocabulary, flashcards, or quizzes.

entries.reviewer_notes: Universal polite greeting. In Bengali, "Nomoshkar" is standard public etiquette. In Urdu, "Adaab" or "Salaam" is common across diverse communities in the Deccan/Karnataka region. Awaiting native reviewer preference for headword display.
Standard expression of gratitude. Note Bengali phonology /o/ rounding in "Dhonnobad". Urdu "Shukriya" is universally used across Karnataka.

entries.english_example: Good morning, have a nice day.

urdu.example_sentence: صبح بخیر، آپ کا دن اچھا گزرے۔
urdu.example_romanization: Subah bakhair, aap ka din accha guzre.

entries.reviewer_notes: Formal morning greetings. In casual everyday conversation, native speakers of both languages frequently use general greetings ("Nomoshkar" / "Salaam") rather than time-specific greetings. Flagged for register review.

Formal honorific address matching Kannada "-ra" suffix. Urdu has gender inflection: "Aap kaise hain?" (masculine/default polite) vs "Aap kaisi hain?" (feminine). In Dakhni Urdu, "Kaise hain ji?" is widespread.

bengali.example_sentence: আমি ভালো আছি, আপনি কেমন আছেন?
bengali.example_romanization: Ami bhalo achi, apni kemon achen?

entries.reviewer_notes: Standard affirmative reply. In colloquial Bengali, subject pronoun "ami" is optionally omitted. In Dakhni Urdu, "Main accha hoon" is also frequent.
Urdu has high register "Barahe karam" and colloquial "Baraye mehrbani". In Dakhni Urdu, "Meharbani karke" or "Zara" is often preferred for daily requests.

bengali.example_sentence: মাফ করবেন, আমার দেরি হয়ে গেল।
bengali.example_romanization: Maaf korben, amar deri hoye gelo.

urdu.example_sentence: معاف کیجیے، مجھے دیر ہو گئی۔
urdu.example_romanization: Maaf kijiye, mujhe der ho gayi.

entries.reviewer_notes: Used for both "Excuse me" (seeking attention) and "Sorry" (apology). Semantically identical to Kannada "Kshamisi".

entries.english_example: I will take leave, see you again.
entries.reviewer_notes: Parting phrases. Note the strong cultural parallel: Kannada "Hogi baruttene" and Bengali "Ekhon ashi" both express "I take leave now with the intention to return". Urdu uses "Phir milenge" or "Khuda/Allah hafiz".

urdu.example_sentence: جی ہاں، یہ میری کتاب ہے۔
urdu.example_romanization: Jee haan, yeh meri kitaab hai.

entries.reviewer_notes: Standard affirmation. Bengali has candrabindu nasalization ("Hyã"). Urdu "Jee haan" denotes respect.

Crucial semantic distinction: Kannada "Illa" denotes both negation ("No") and absence ("Not there/Not available"). Bengali splits this into "Na" (negation) and "Nei" (absence). Urdu uses "Nahin" vs "Nahin hai". Reviewer must confirm best presentation.

Dative subject construction matching Kannada "Nanage neeru beku". Colloquial Bengali "Amar jol lagbe" directly parallels Kannada syntax. In Dakhni Urdu, "Hona" ("Mereku paani hona") is a famous local mirror of Dravidian "Beku".
Polite refusal of items/service. In Dakhni Urdu in Bangalore/Mysore, "Nako" ("Shakkar nako") is universally used as the exact functional equivalent of Kannada "Beda".
Bengali lexical nuance: "Chena/Chini" is specifically used for knowing/recognizing roads, places, and people, while "Jana" is used for facts/information.

entries.english_example: I do not know their name.

urdu.example_sentence: مجھے اس بارے میں پتا نہیں ہے۔
urdu.example_romanization: Mujhe is baare mein pata nahin hai.

entries.reviewer_notes: Negative knowledge. In everyday Urdu, "Pata nahin" is common; in Dakhni Urdu, "Nai maaloom" is very standard.

urdu.example_sentence: ٹھیک ہے، ویسا ہی کرتے ہیں۔
urdu.example_romanization: Theek hai, waisa hi karte hain.

entries.reviewer_notes: Everyday agreement/acknowledgment. Notice historical cognate: Urdu "Sahi" and Kannada "Sari".
Quantifier/intensifier adverb matching Kannada "Tumba". Bengali uses "Khub" (very) and "Onek" (a lot/many).
Cardinal number 1. Bengali uses numerical classifier suffix "-ti" / "-ta" for objects ("ekti coffee").
Cardinal number 2. Bengali "duto" (two items).
Cardinal number 3. Bengali human classifier "-jon" ("tinjon").
Cardinal number 4.
Cardinal number 5. Bengali has nasalized vowel with candrabindu.
Cardinal number 10. Note Bengali rounded vowel pronunciation "Dosh" vs Urdu "Das".
Cardinal number 20. In Bengali, indigenous "Kuri" is common in daily markets alongside Sanskrit-derived "Bish".
Cardinal number 100. Bengali "Eksho" vs Urdu "Sau".

Cultural greeting context: In Karnataka, asking "Oota aayta?" is a warm greeting equivalent to "How are you?". Both Bengali "Khaoa hoyeche?" and Urdu "Khaana ho gaya?" carry this exact hospitality sentiment.

Kannada "Tindi" covers breakfast and snacks/tiffin. In Bengali, "Jolkhabar" is traditional West Bengal standard; "Nasta" is common across communities and regions. Urdu "Naashta" strictly refers to breakfast.
Dialectal sensitivity: Bengali speakers in West Bengal predominantly use "Jol", while Bengali speakers in Bangladesh and Muslim communities commonly use "Pani". Both are noted for inclusive learning.

bengali.example_sentence: এক কাপ গরম ফিল্টার কফি দিন।
bengali.example_romanization: Ek cup gorom filter coffee din.

entries.reviewer_notes: Loanword universally understood in darshinis and cafes across Karnataka.
Colloquial vs formal: Bengali "Bhalo shaad" or "Khabar khub bhalo" is everyday; "Shushwadu" is textbook. In Urdu, "Mazedaar" is standard everyday; "Lazeez" is formal.
Temperature descriptor. Both Bengali "Gorom" and Urdu "Garam" share cognate roots.
Location interrogative.
Honorific imperative "Go" ("Jan" / "Jaiye") vs cohortative "Let's go" ("Cholun" / "Chalein"). Matches Kannada dual usage of "Hogi" (Go) and "Hogona" (Let us go).
Respectful invitation to enter or come, matching Kannada "Banni". In Dakhni Urdu: "Aao ji / Aaiye".
Spatial proximity near.

urdu.example_sentence: ایئرپورٹ یہاں سے بہت دور ہے۔
urdu.example_romanization: Airport yahan se bahut door hai.

entries.reviewer_notes: Spatial distance far.
Transit instruction for autos and taxis. In Dakhni Urdu in Bangalore/Mysore, "Yahan roko ji" or "Yahan rok dijiye" is the exact street vernacular.
Price and quantity question interrogative.

entries.english_example: The price of this is high.
entries.reviewer_notes: Price noun.

urdu.example_sentence: براہِ کرم قیمت تھوڑی کم کیجیے۔
urdu.example_romanization: Barahe karam qeemat thodi kam kijiye.

entries.reviewer_notes: Market bargaining phrase. In Dakhni Urdu, "Thoda kam karo ji" is common in market interactions.
Proximal demonstrative pronoun this.
Distal demonstrative pronoun that.

entries.english_example: Do you have change for 100 rupees?

urdu.example_sentence: پانچ سو روپے کے کھلے ہیں؟
urdu.example_romanization: Paanch sau rupaye ke khule hain?

entries.reviewer_notes: Inquiry for small currency/change. Bengali specifically uses "Khuchro"; Urdu uses "Khule paise" or "Rezgari" / "Chillar" (shared Deccan slang).

urdu.example_sentence: سلام، آپ کا نام کیا ہے؟
urdu.example_romanization: Salaam, aap ka naam kya hai?

entries.reviewer_notes: Polite name inquiry.
Time inquiry. Bengali idiomatically asks "Kota baje?" (How many strikes have rung?).
Interrogative reason why.
Time interrogative when.
Manner interrogative how.

entries.english_example: How are you, what is the latest news?
entries.reviewer_notes: Casual inquiry matching Kannada "Enu samachara?".

entries.english_example: Sorry, I only know a little Kannada.

bengali.example_sentence: মাফ করবেন, আমি একটু কন্নড় জানি।
bengali.example_romanization: Maaf korben, ami ektu Kannada jani.

urdu.example_sentence: معاف کیجیے، مجھے تھوڑی کنڑ آتی ہے۔
urdu.example_romanization: Maaf kijiye, mujhe thodi Kannada aati hai.

entries.reviewer_notes: Critical beginner sentence. Notice in Urdu: "Kannada aati hai" uses feminine agreement for language.

entries.english_example: I am learning Kannada, please help me.

bengali.example_sentence: আমি কন্নড় শিখছি, একটু সাহায্য করুন।
bengali.example_romanization: Ami Kannada shikhchi, ektu shahajjo korun.

urdu.example_sentence: میں کنڑ سیکھ رہا ہوں، مدد کیجیے۔
urdu.example_romanization: Main Kannada seekh raha hoon, madad kijiye.

entries.reviewer_notes: Urdu gender agreement note: Male speaker: "seekh raha hoon"; Female speaker: "seekh rahi hoon". Reviewer should confirm if dual form display is preferred.

bengali.example_sentence: দয়া করে একটু আস্তে কথা বলুন।
bengali.example_romanization: Doya kore ektu aaste kotha bolun.

entries.reviewer_notes: Pacing request for learners.

bengali.example_sentence: দয়া করে আমাকে একটু সাহায্য করুন।
bengali.example_romanization: Doya kore amake ektu shahajjo korun.

urdu.example_sentence: براہِ کرم میری تھوڑی مدد کیجیے۔
urdu.example_romanization: Barahe karam meri thodi madad kijiye.

entries.reviewer_notes: Polite help request.

urdu.example_sentence: معاف کیجیے، مجھے سمجھ نہیں آیا۔
urdu.example_romanization: Maaf kijiye, mujhe samajh nahin aaya.

entries.reviewer_notes: Comprehension clarification.

urdu.example_sentence: کرناٹک اور بنگلور بہت خوبصورت ہیں۔
urdu.example_romanization: Karnataka aur Bengaluru bahut khoobsurat hain.

entries.reviewer_notes: Appreciation expression. Both Bengali and Urdu forms express natural admiration for Bengaluru and Karnataka.
